lessonTitle: Skin Cancer: BCC, SCC, Melanoma, ABCDE Assessment, Ultraviolet Light and Breslow Thickness

blocks.text: A 52-year-old farmer who has worked outdoors for three decades notices a pearly, slowly enlarging bump beside his nose that bleeds when he dries his face. At the same visit his wife asks about a dark mole on her calf that has grown over the past year. One lesion is a skin cancer that almost never spreads; the other, if it is what she fears, can be lethal. Telling them apart is a central skill of clinical medicine.

blocks.markdown: The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium. **Keratinocytes** arise from basal cells and mature upward through the squamous layers to the keratinised surface, while **melanocytes** in the basal layer make melanin pigment that shields nuclei from ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Skin cancers are named by their cell of origin: **basal cell carcinoma (BCC)** and **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)** arise from keratinocytes (together called non-melanoma skin cancer, the commonest cancers in fair-skinned populations), and **melanoma** arises from melanocytes.

rows: Pearly papule or nodule with telangiectasia and rolled edge; central ulcer ('rodent ulcer')
Firm, scaly or crusted nodule or ulcer; may arise from actinic keratosis
Pigmented lesion that is asymmetric, irregular, multicoloured and changing; may be amelanotic
Sun-exposed face, especially around the nose
Sun-exposed sites: ears, lips, dorsum of hands, scalp
Any site, including back in men and legs in women
Slow, locally invasive and destructive; metastasis extremely rare
Locally invasive; can metastasise to regional nodes, more likely at lip, ear or in immunosuppression
Aggressive; metastasises early by lymphatics and blood
Chronic UV exposure, immunosuppression, actinic keratoses
Intermittent intense UV (sunburn), many naevi, fair skin, family history
blocks.caption: Skin cancers differentiated by behaviour

blocks.title: Reasoning from behaviour
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old kidney transplant recipient has a rapidly growing, crusted nodule on the helix of his ear. A fair-skinned 50-year-old has a pearly papule with fine blood vessels on the cheek that has grown slowly over two years. Which is likely to be SCC and which BCC, and why does the distinction matter?

steps.text: The ear nodule is firm, crusted, rapidly growing and in an immunosuppressed patient on a high-risk site: this fits SCC.
A slow pearly papule with telangiectasia on the face is typical of BCC.

BCC is locally destructive but virtually never metastasises, so complete local excision cures it. SCC, particularly at the ear or in immunosuppression, can spread to nodes, so excision and assessment of nodes matter more.

blocks.answer: Ear nodule: SCC; cheek papule: BCC. SCC has metastatic potential whereas BCC is almost purely local.

blocks.markdown:
### The ABCDE criteria for pigmented lesions

The **ABCDE** checklist helps to identify melanoma in a pigmented lesion: **A**symmetry (the two halves do not match); **B**order irregularity (notched, scalloped or blurred edges); **C**olour variation (several shades of brown, black, red, white or blue); **D**iameter greater than 6 mm (a pencil eraser), although melanomas can be smaller; and **E**volving (any change in size, shape, colour, elevation, or new symptoms such as bleeding or itch). **Evolution** is regarded as the most important single feature. A lesion that satisfies one or more criteria should prompt referral, and the suspected lesion is removed by **complete excision biopsy** with a narrow margin so that the full thickness can be measured, rather than by partial sampling. The **number needed to excise** (benign plus malignant lesions removed, divided by melanomas found) measures how selective a clinician is.

blocks.title: Applying ABCDE
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old woman has an 8 mm mole on her back with a notched edge, areas of black and brown, and it has darkened over the last 6 months. Apply ABCDE and decide what to do.

steps.text: Border: notched edge, abnormal. Colour: two shades, black and brown, abnormal. Diameter: 8 mm exceeds 6 mm. Evolving: darkened over 6 months, abnormal. Asymmetry would also be assessed.
At least four features are present, so the lesion is suspicious for melanoma.
Refer urgently for complete excision biopsy with a narrow margin and histology, which gives the Breslow thickness that determines further management.

blocks.answer: Highly suspicious for melanoma; urgent excision biopsy.

blocks.markdown:
### Ultraviolet radiation

UV radiation is the main environmental cause of all three skin cancers. **UVB** (280-315 nm) is absorbed in the epidermis and is directly mutagenic: it joins adjacent pyrimidines to form **cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers**, producing characteristic C-to-T mutations (the 'UV signature') in genes such as **TP53**. **UVA** penetrates deeper and damages DNA indirectly through reactive oxygen species. Chronic cumulative exposure is linked to SCC and BCC (BCC driven by mutations in the Hedgehog pathway gene PTCH1), whereas **intermittent intense exposure with sunburn**, especially in childhood, is linked to melanoma. Fair skin (Fitzpatrick types I and II), red hair and many naevi increase risk. Sun protection works by reducing the UV dose reaching the skin.

blocks.caption: Sun protection factor (SPF) approximates the multiple by which the UV dose needed to cause redness is increased when sunscreen is applied adequately.

blocks.markdown:
### Breslow thickness

The single most important prognostic factor in localised melanoma is the **Breslow thickness**: the vertical depth in millimetres from the top of the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest invasive tumour cell. Deeper tumours have greater access to dermal lymphatics and vessels and are more likely to have metastasised. Thickness determines the width of surgical re-excision and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered.

rows: Best prognosis; wide local excision, sentinel node biopsy only in selected cases
Higher risk of nodal and distant spread
blocks.caption: Breslow thickness and T category in melanoma staging

blocks.title: Interpreting Breslow thickness
blocks.prompt: Histology reports one melanoma with Breslow thickness 0.6 mm and another with 3.4 mm. Compare their prognosis.

steps.text: 0.6 mm is within T1 (1.0 mm or less), so the tumour is thin, has limited access to lymphatics and carries an excellent prognosis after wide excision.
3.4 mm is T3 (over 2.0 to 4.0 mm), a thick tumour with a substantially higher risk of nodal and distant metastasis.
The thicker tumour needs wider excision, staging assessment such as sentinel node biopsy, and closer follow-up.

blocks.answer: The 0.6 mm melanoma has a far better prognosis than the 3.4 mm melanoma.

points: BCC is pearly, slowly growing and locally invasive with negligible metastasis, SCC is scaly or crusted with real metastatic potential, and melanoma arises from melanocytes and spreads early.
ABCDE (asymmetry, border, colour, diameter above 6 mm, evolving) screens pigmented lesions, with evolution the most important and complete excision biopsy needed for suspicious ones.
UVB causes pyrimidine dimers and TP53 mutations, intermittent intense sun exposure is linked to melanoma, and Breslow thickness is the strongest prognostic factor in localised melanoma.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a slowly growing pearly papule with surface telangiectasia and a rolled edge on his cheek. Which statement about this tumour is correct?

options.text: It is locally invasive but metastasises very rarely
It commonly metastasises to the lungs early
It arises from melanocytes
It always arises from an actinic keratosis

questions.correctOptionText: It is locally invasive but metastasises very rarely

distractorRationale.a: Correct: BCC grows locally and destructively but almost never metastasises.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: early lung metastasis is a feature of aggressive tumours such as melanoma.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: BCC arises from basal keratinocytes.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: actinic keratosis is the precursor of SCC.

questions.explanation: A pearly papule with telangiectasia and a rolled edge is typical of basal cell carcinoma. It invades locally, so treatment is complete excision, and metastasis is extremely uncommon.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old heart transplant recipient on long-term immunosuppression develops a rapidly growing keratotic nodule on his lower lip. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma is likely, and it has potential to metastasise to regional lymph nodes
It is a basal cell carcinoma that cannot spread
It is a melanoma because it is growing quickly
It is a benign naevus

questions.correctOptionText: Squamous cell carcinoma is likely, and it has potential to metastasise to regional lymph nodes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: SCC is more common and more aggressive in immunosuppressed patients, particularly on the lip.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: BCC does not usually appear this way and is not the type that behaves aggressively.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a keratotic nodule suggests keratinocyte, not melanocyte, origin.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: rapid growth argues against a benign naevus.

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression and sun exposure increase the risk of SCC, which can metastasise to regional nodes, especially at the lip and ear. Prompt biopsy and excision are needed.

questions.stem: In the ABCDE assessment of a pigmented lesion, what does the letter D refer to?

options.text: Diameter greater than 6 mm
Depth below 1 mm
Dermatomal distribution
Duration over 10 years

distractorRationale.a: Correct: D stands for diameter above about 6 mm.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: depth is measured later, as Breslow thickness, on histology.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: dermatomal distribution applies to shingles.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: duration is not part of ABCDE, although change over time is covered by E.

questions.explanation: The D in ABCDE refers to diameter exceeding 6 mm, about the size of a pencil eraser. Melanomas may be smaller, which is why evolution is considered more important.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has a 5 mm brown mole on his shoulder, symmetrical with regular borders and uniform colour, but his wife says it has become raised and itchy over 3 months. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Evolution is a concerning feature even without other criteria, so the lesion needs expert assessment
Reassure, because it is under 6 mm
Reassure, because it is symmetrical
Treat as a basal cell carcinoma

questions.correctOptionText: Evolution is a concerning feature even without other criteria, so the lesion needs expert assessment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: change over time is the most important warning sign, and small melanomas exist.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: melanomas can be under 6 mm.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: early melanomas may be symmetrical.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a changing pigmented lesion is not a pearly BCC.

questions.explanation: Evolving lesions, with change in size, elevation or symptoms such as itch, should be evaluated even if other criteria are not met. A lesion of this size can still be an early melanoma.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains how UVB radiation initiates skin cancer?

options.text: Formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers in DNA, leading to mutations such as in TP53
Direct activation of the Philadelphia chromosome
Depletion of melanin synthesis in the dermis
Inhibition of keratinocyte apoptosis by vitamin D

questions.correctOptionText: Formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers in DNA, leading to mutations such as in TP53

distractorRationale.a: Correct: UVB directly crosslinks adjacent pyrimidines, causing characteristic mutations if not repaired.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the Philadelphia chromosome is a feature of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: melanin synthesis occurs in the epidermis and is protective.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is not the mechanism.

questions.explanation: UVB produces pyrimidine dimers that, if misrepaired, cause C-to-T mutations. Mutated TP53 allows damaged keratinocytes to survive and expand, leading to SCC.

questions.stem: A dermatology clinic excises 240 pigmented lesions in a year, and histology confirms melanoma in 30 of them. Calculate the number needed to excise (lesions excised per melanoma found).
questions.explanation: The number needed to excise is the total excised divided by the number of melanomas: 240 / 30 = 8. It measures how selective clinical assessment is, since a lower number means fewer benign lesions removed per melanoma found.

questions.stem: A sunscreen of SPF 30 is applied adequately. Using the approximation that the fraction of UVB reaching the skin is 1/SPF, calculate the percentage of UVB transmitted.
questions.explanation: 1 / 30 = 0.0333, so about 3.3% of UVB is transmitted, meaning about 96.7% is blocked. Real-world protection is lower because sunscreen is usually applied too thinly and wears off.

questions.stem: Differentiate basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma by cell of origin, appearance and behaviour.
markingGuide: BCC: basal keratinocytes; pearly papule with telangiectasia, rolled edge, central ulcer; locally invasive, metastasis very rare
SCC: squamous keratinocytes; scaly, crusted or ulcerated nodule, may arise from actinic keratosis; can metastasise to nodes, especially lip, ear and immunosuppressed
Melanoma: melanocytes; changing irregular pigmented lesion; early lymphatic and haematogenous metastasis
Link between behaviour and management: complete excision cures BCC, SCC requires attention to nodal spread, melanoma depends on thickness
questions.explanation: Cell of origin determines appearance and biological behaviour. The risk of spread is lowest in BCC, intermediate in SCC and highest in melanoma, which shapes the urgency and extent of treatment.

questions.stem: Explain each component of the ABCDE criteria for assessing a pigmented lesion, say which feature is considered the most important, and explain why a suspected melanoma should be removed by complete excision biopsy rather than a partial sample.
markingGuide: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving
Evolution (change in size, shape, colour, elevation, symptoms) is the most important
Melanomas can be smaller than 6 mm
Complete excision biopsy with narrow margin allows the pathologist to examine the whole lesion
This allows accurate measurement of Breslow thickness, which determines further excision and staging
Partial sampling may miss the thickest area and mislead
questions.explanation: The criteria encode the features of unregulated growth and heterogeneous pigment production. Accurate histological staging depends on examining the whole lesion, so the full thickness can be measured.

questions.stem: Explain the role of ultraviolet radiation in the pathogenesis of skin cancer, contrasting the exposure patterns linked to melanoma and to non-melanoma skin cancer, and explain why Breslow thickness is the main prognostic factor in melanoma.
markingGuide: UVB forms cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers causing C-to-T mutations in genes such as TP53; UVA acts through reactive oxygen species
Chronic cumulative exposure linked to SCC and BCC
Intermittent intense exposure with sunburn, especially in childhood, linked to melanoma
Risk factors: fair skin, many naevi, immunosuppression
Breslow thickness: depth in mm from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell
Greater depth gives greater access to dermal lymphatics and blood vessels and higher risk of metastasis; it guides excision margin and sentinel node biopsy
questions.explanation: UV damage to DNA produces mutations that drive tumour initiation. The depth of invasion at diagnosis reflects how far the tumour has progressed towards the vessels that carry it to distant sites, so it is the strongest predictor of outcome.
